title: Banning Sugary Food at Checkouts Cuts Soda Sales
paragraphs: You're waiting in line at a store when a bottle of soda catches your eye. You weren't planning to buy it, but suddenly it's in your basket.
That's exactly why these products are often placed near the checkout — they're easy to notice while shoppers are waiting, and can encourage impulse buying.
But in Berkeley, California, many sugary treats have disappeared from checkout areas.
In March 2021, Berkeley became the first city in the world to introduce a mandatory "healthy checkout" policy.

As part of the policy, large stores had to stop displaying drinks and foods high in added sugar at checkouts. And from January 2022, the city could take action against stores that didn't follow these rules.
Having too much added sugar, particularly from sugary drinks, has been linked to health problems such as heart disease and tooth decay.

And in the US, sugary drinks are popular with both adults and young people. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention collected between 2011 and 2014, about half of adults and six in 10 young people had a sugary drink each day.
Now, a new study has looked at whether Berkeley's policy has changed what people buy.

Researchers looked at sales from 71 stores in Berkeley and three other California cities between 2019 and 2023. They found that soda sales fell more in Berkeley after the policy became enforceable than they did in the other cities.
However, the policy doesn't stop stores from selling sugary drinks altogether — it only controls what stores can display at checkouts, so soda can still be sold elsewhere in the store.
And not every sugary product saw the same change — overall candy sales didn't fall after the policy was enforced, although supermarkets sold less candy in small packages.
But for soda, at least, what shoppers see at the checkout does seem to matter.
